explanations.explanation: Asaph sings, “Hear us, O Shepherd of Israel, who leads Joseph like a flock…” A flock needs somebody out front, and that's the name he reaches for. Sheep don't pick their own route, baker, and I know a few stamper-shaped folks who get lost in a kitchen. Good to have a Shepherd who leads.
Rock isn't the name Asaph uses in this verse. He says God “…leads Joseph like a flock…” and he calls Him Shepherd of Israel. Look for the name that goes with the sheep.

Light is close to the mood of this song, since Asaph asks God to “shine forth” in the same verse. But the name he calls Him is Shepherd, because he's picturing a flock. The shining is what he asks for, and the title is what he calls God. Keep those two apart and you're golden.

explanations.answer: Rally it and come save us
explanations.explanation: Asaph prays, “Rally Your mighty power and come to save us.” He doesn't ask God to send help from a distance. He asks God to come Himself. That's a man who knows exactly who he's calling.

explanations.answer: Hold it back a while longer
explanations.explanation: This one's the opposite of the prayer, baker. Asaph says, “Rally Your mighty power and come to save us.” Nobody stands in the kitchen shouting for the oven to wait. He's asking for God's power to move.

explanations.answer: Turn it on the far mountains
explanations.explanation: The far mountains don't show up in this verse. Asaph asks God to “Rally Your mighty power and come to save us.” His eyes are on his own people, not on faraway scenery. He wants that power aimed at saving them.

Asaph prays, “Restore us, O God, and cause Your face to shine upon us, that we may be saved.” The last part of the sentence is the reason he gives for the asking. Saved is where this prayer is headed. You read it right, friend.

Close, but the verse says otherwise. Asaph prays, “Restore us, O God, and cause Your face to shine upon us, that we may be saved.” That last bit, “…that we may be saved.” is right there in the line. So the answer is True, baker.

explanations.answer: His anger smoldering against their prayers
explanations.explanation: Asaph asks, “O LORD God of Hosts, how long will Your anger smolder against the prayers of Your people?” Smolder is a good word, because it's a slow burn and not a blaze. And notice whose prayers these are: His own people's. That's the question hanging over the whole song.

explanations.answer: The famine spreading across the land
explanations.explanation: There's no famine in this verse, baker. Asaph asks, “O LORD God of Hosts, how long will Your anger smolder against the prayers of Your people?” His how long is about God's anger and the prayers going up. I know a famine would make a fine question, but it's not what's on the page.

explanations.answer: The war with the armies of Egypt
explanations.explanation: No war with Egypt shows up here. Asaph asks, “O LORD God of Hosts, how long will Your anger smolder against the prayers of Your people?” Egypt does come up later in the song, but as the place a vine was pulled up from (Psalm 80:8). This verse is all about the smoldering anger.

explanations.answer: Bread of tears and tears to drink
explanations.explanation: Asaph says, “You fed them with the bread of tears and made them drink the full measure of their tears.” Tears for the meal and tears for the drink. I think that's a song written by someone who has cried a lot, and the verse is heavy.

explanations.answer: Ashes for bread and bitter water
explanations.explanation: Ashes and bitter water sound like they'd fit, but they aren't what Asaph says. He says, “You fed them with the bread of tears and made them drink the full measure of their tears.” Tears are both the bread and the drink. That's what makes the line so sad.

Bitter herbs and vinegar don't appear in this psalm. Asaph says, “You fed them with the bread of tears and made them drink the full measure of their tears.” Tears are the whole menu, baker. It's a sad meal, and the verse is a heavy one.

Asaph says, “You make us contend with our neighbors; our enemies mock us.” Mocking stings in its own way, baker. I've heard my share of jokes about a stamper with a mustache for hands, but I got to laugh along. That's a different kind of mocking than this verse.
Fear is a fair guess, but it's not what the verse says. Asaph says, “our enemies mock us.” Fear isn't the word he uses. What the enemies do is mock.
Avoiding would at least be quiet, baker. But Asaph says, “our enemies mock us.” These enemies are paying very close attention, and what they do with it is mock.
Asaph sings, “You uprooted a vine from Egypt; You drove out the nations and transplanted it.” Egypt is the place God pulled the vine up from. And God does the pulling up and the planting Himself.
Babylon isn't named anywhere in this psalm. Asaph says, “You uprooted a vine from Egypt…” Egypt is the place God pulled it up from, and then He transplanted it.
Assyria doesn't make an appearance in this song, baker. Asaph says, “You uprooted a vine from Egypt…” It's Egypt that the vine is pulled up from. Quite the move.

I see why that sounds right, but the verse says something else. Asaph says, “You drove out the nations and transplanted it.” So there were nations in that land, and God drove them out first. The land wasn't empty, so the answer is False.

Right, baker. Asaph says, “You drove out the nations and transplanted it.” The land had nations in it, and God drove them out before the vine went in. It's the one thing the verse spells out about where the vine got planted.

Asaph says of the vine, “You cleared the ground for it, and it took root and filled the land.” Roots first, then everything else. Plants don't skip that step. The ground was cleared and the vine took root.
A vine with wings would be something, baker. Picture it flapping across the land. But Asaph says it “…took root and filled the land.” Roots, not wings.
Shelter is a nice thought, and a vine does give shade in the next verse. But this verse says the vine “…took root and filled the land.” The word that goes in the blank is root.
Asaph says, “It sent out its branches to the Sea, and its shoots toward the River.” The vine reaches all the way to the Sea. That's a vine with ambition, baker.

The Jordan isn't named in this verse. Asaph says, “It sent out its branches to the Sea, and its shoots toward the River.” The branches reach the Sea, and the shoots go toward the River. Good guess for a river, but it's the Sea in the blank.
The Negev doesn't show up in this psalm. Asaph says, “It sent out its branches to the Sea, and its shoots toward the River.” The word for the blank is Sea. This vine is stretching out, baker.

Not quite, friend. Asaph asks, “Why have You broken down its walls, so that all who pass by pick its fruit?” He says “You,” and that's God he's talking to. The verse doesn't name enemies as the ones who broke them. So the answer is False.

Right. Asaph asks, “Why have You broken down its walls, so that all who pass by pick its fruit?” He's speaking to God, and he says “You.” The verse never says enemies knocked the walls down. That's why it's such a heavy WHY.
Asaph says, “The boar from the forest ravages it, and the creatures of the field feed upon it.” It's a boar, and it comes out of the forest. With the walls down, nothing's keeping it out.
A lion would be a dramatic choice, baker. But Asaph says, “The boar from the forest ravages it…” The animal in this verse is a boar. The creatures of the field come along to eat, too.

A bear would scare me, I'll admit. But the verse says, “The boar from the forest ravages it, and the creatures of the field feed upon it.” The one that comes from the forest is a boar. Nobody's bringing a bear into this song.

Asaph prays, “Return, O God of Hosts, we pray! Look down from heaven and see! Attend to this vine…” Return, look, attend: he stacks up the asks fast. I think he's piling them on because he's desperate, and I'd pray just as fast with smoke pouring out of my oven. Heaven is the word that fills the blank.
Zion is a good guess, baker, but it isn't in this psalm. Asaph prays, “Look down from heaven and see!” Heaven is the place God looks down from. He wants Him to see the vine and attend to it.
Sinai doesn't come up anywhere in this song. Asaph prays, “Look down from heaven and see!” He asks God to look down from heaven and to attend to the vine. That's the word for the blank.

Asaph prays, “Let Your hand be upon the man at Your right hand, on the son of man You have raised up for Yourself.” The man is at God's right hand, and Asaph says God raised him up for Himself. That's the place the verse names, baker.
David's throne isn't named in this psalm. Asaph says, “Let Your hand be upon the man at Your right hand…” The man is described as the one at God's right hand. That's the answer, baker.

The city gate isn't in this song. Asaph prays, “Let Your hand be upon the man at Your right hand, on the son of man You have raised up for Yourself.” The man is at God's right hand. No gates anywhere.
Asaph says, “Then we will not turn away from You; revive us, and we will call on Your name.” The people say they will not turn away from God. It's a promise inside a prayer. You're right, baker.
Not this time, friend. Asaph says, “Then we will not turn away from You; revive us, and we will call on Your name.” The people say they will not turn away from God. So the answer is True.
Asaph says, “revive us, and we will call on Your name.” That's what he promises if God revives them. I think it's a lovely thing to promise, baker.

An altar isn't in this psalm, baker. Asaph says, “revive us, and we will call on Your name.” Building an altar sounds like a big project, and I get lost assembling a shelf without the instructions. What they promise is to call on His name.
No marching in this verse. Asaph says, “revive us, and we will call on Your name.” What they promise to do is call on God's name. That's a prayer, not a battle plan.
